25-minute-pomodoro-focus-sprints.title: Use a Focus Block and a Short Break
25-minute-pomodoro-focus-sprints.description: Work on one defined task for a bounded block, take a real break, and adjust the next block from fatigue, interruption, and restart observations rather than treating one schedule as universal.
25-minute-pomodoro-focus-sprints.reason: A micro-break meta-analysis supports bounded well-being claims for short breaks but not a universal twenty-five-minute schedule or general performance gain. Rewrite and keep practical.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Choose one task, work in a bounded focus block, then take a short break that actually changes posture, attention, or activity.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Define the result for this block and remove avoidable interruptions. Work until the chosen stopping cue, then step away from the task. Before starting again, note fatigue, unfinished context, and whether a shorter or longer next block would fit better.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did the block help me advance one task, did the break reduce fatigue, and what duration or boundary should I change next time?

faq.question: Must the focus block last twenty-five minutes?
faq.answer: No. Use a duration that fits the task, your current capacity, and the cost of interruption. The timing is a planning choice, not a universal optimum.

faq.question: What counts as a break?
faq.answer: Pause the task and change activity. Stand, move, rest your eyes, get water, or sit quietly rather than replacing one demanding screen task with another.

faq.question: When should I stop using timed blocks?
faq.answer: Stop or change the method when the timer fragments work, adds pressure, masks significant fatigue, or conflicts with safety and health needs.

intro.html: A focus timer is a boundary, not a scientific promise. Use it to make one task concrete, protect a work interval, and create a deliberate break. Adjust the next block from what you observe.

sections.title: 1. Define one result
sections.html: Name the task and the visible result for the block. Close or mute interruptions that are not required for that result.

sections.title: 2. Work to the chosen boundary
sections.html: Use a timer, a task milestone, or another clear stopping cue. If you are repeatedly blocked, stop and clarify the next action instead of waiting for the timer to rescue the task.

sections.title: 3. Take a real break and adjust
sections.html: Change posture, attention, or activity. Before the next block, note fatigue, lost context, and restart difficulty, then keep or change the duration.

active-listening-exercises.title: Paraphrase, Check, and Ask One Follow-up
active-listening-exercises.description: Listen to one point without preparing a rebuttal, paraphrase it in neutral language, ask whether you understood correctly, and then ask one relevant follow-up.
active-listening-exercises.reason: A controlled study supports a narrow perceived-understanding claim in initial interactions, not broad conflict, therapy, trust, or relationship outcomes. Rewrite and keep practical.
forbidden_public_fragments: Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: After the speaker finishes one point, paraphrase the meaning, check accuracy, and ask one follow-up before giving advice or defending your position.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Ask whether the person wants listening, advice, or a decision. Let them finish one point. Restate the meaning without adding motive, then ask whether you understood. Use one open follow-up only if they want to continue. Set a boundary or pause when the conversation becomes unsafe or unproductive.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did the speaker confirm my paraphrase, what did the follow-up clarify, and was listening still the right response?

faq.question: Does paraphrasing mean I agree?
faq.answer: No. It checks understanding. You can disagree after the speaker confirms that you represented the point accurately.

faq.question: What if the paraphrase sounds mechanical?
faq.answer: Use ordinary language and keep it short. If the person wants direct action rather than reflection, ask what kind of response would be useful.

faq.question: When is listening not enough?
faq.answer: Listening does not replace a decision, boundary, emergency response, professional help, or action against unsafe behavior.

intro.html: Active listening is a small accuracy practice, not a guarantee of agreement or repair. The useful loop is to hear one point, paraphrase it, check the meaning, and ask one relevant question.

sections.title: 1. Ask what response is needed
sections.html: Clarify whether the person wants to be heard, receive advice, make a decision, or solve a specific problem.

sections.title: 2. Paraphrase and check
sections.html: Restate the meaning in neutral language and ask whether you understood. Correct the paraphrase rather than defending it.

sections.title: 3. Ask one follow-up or set a boundary
sections.html: Ask one question that clarifies the situation. Pause or change the response when the conversation requires action, a boundary, or safety support.
